title: The Perry Preschool Children at Forty
text:
In the early 1960s, in Ypsilanti, Michigan, the school administrator David Weikart was worried about how many poor Black children in his district were failing at school. He and his colleagues started a preschool program at the Perry Elementary School and, unusually for the time, designed it as an experiment.

Between 1962 and 1967, 123 three and four-year-olds from low-income African American families were divided into two groups. One group attended a high-quality preschool for two and a half hours each weekday, mostly over two school years, with small classes and well-trained teachers who encouraged children to plan, carry out and review their own activities. Teachers also visited each child's home once a week to work with the mother and child together. The other group received no preschool.

The researchers kept following the participants for decades. In 2005, Lawrence Schweinhart and colleagues reported results at age 40. Those who had attended the program were more likely to have graduated from high school, had higher median earnings, were more likely to own a home, and had been arrested fewer times than those in the comparison group.

The Perry study became one of the most cited arguments for investing in early childhood education, especially through the analyses of the economist James Heckman.
lesson: Help given early to a child and a family can pay off for a lifetime. Small, well-designed support in the first years matters a great deal.
people: David Weikart, Lawrence Schweinhart and colleagues
source: Schweinhart, L. J., Montie, J., Xiang, Z., Barnett, W. S., Belfield, C. R., and Nores, M. (2005). Lifetime Effects: The High/Scope Perry Preschool Study Through Age 40. Ypsilanti, MI: High/Scope Press.
caveat: The sample was small and the assignment process was not perfectly random, so the size of the effects is debated even though reanalyses support the main conclusions.
